analysis.investment_thesis: EIH is an exceptional business — India's most iconic luxury hotel brand with pristine balance sheet and 38.9% operating margins — but at 17.86x EV/EBITDA and a 1.7% FCF yield, the price already reflects near-perfection, leaving no margin of safety for a fundamentally cyclical business. The consensus loves this story; that's precisely when I grow cautious.
key_strengths: Irreplaceable Oberoi brand with genuine pricing power — luxury positioning insulates margins far above industry peers (38.9% operating margin)
Near-debt-free fortress balance sheet: D/E of 0.05, borrowings contracted from INR 647 Cr (2020) to INR 250 Cr (2025) even through COVID
Exceptional capital discipline through cycle — ROCE of 23.4% and net profit CAGR of 20.6% over 9 years despite a catastrophic 2021-22
key_risks: FCF yield of just 1.7% (INR 346 Cr FCF / INR 20,130 Cr market cap) — well below my 6-8% minimum; investor is paying a steep toll for quality
Capex surged to INR 485 Cr in FY25 (up 118% YoY) and CWIP hit INR 403 Cr — expansion is compressing free cash at precisely the moment the cycle may be peaking
COVID proved revenues can collapse 75% in a single year (INR 1,596 Cr → INR 494 Cr); at 26.5x P/E, the market prices zero recurrence of any disruption
red_flags: FCF yield of ~1.7% signals the market has priced in a very long runway of prosperity with no room for error
Promoter holding of only 32.85% is low for a family-controlled luxury brand — skin-in-the-game is limited relative to reputation
Capex doubling in one year while FCF declines from INR 494 Cr to INR 346 Cr — growth is being funded at the cost of current shareholder returns
analysis.detailed_analysis:
EIH is unquestionably a high-quality business — the Oberoi brand is arguably India's most defensible hospitality asset, and the numbers prove it. Operating margins of 38.9%, ROCE of 23.4%, and a D/E ratio of 0.05 after navigating COVID without a rights issue or distress are genuinely impressive. The post-COVID recovery has been sharp: EBITDA went from INR -225 Cr in FY21 to INR 1,298 Cr in FY25. I have no quarrel with the business. My quarrel is entirely with the price.

Second-level thinking demands I ask: what does INR 20,130 Cr market cap already assume? At 17.86x EV/EBITDA and 26.5x P/E, it assumes that FY25's record margins persist, that the capex cycle (INR 485 Cr spent, INR 403 Cr in CWIP) delivers returns without delay, and that no macro shock — rupee depreciation, geopolitical disruption, a sharp slowdown in business travel — interrupts the story. FCF yield of 1.7% means I wait 58 years to get my money back in cash terms unless the multiple re-rates higher. The stress scenario is ugly: a 30% revenue decline (far less severe than COVID) would devastate earnings at this operating leverage, and with the stock priced for perfection, the downside is asymmetrically worse than the upside. Own it if you must, but don't buy more here.
